name: Demo — what makes a weeknight dinner feel easy
note: A tiny synthetic example (3 short interviews + one photo note), made up to show how the tool works.

sources.name: D1 — interview
paragraphs: Interviewer: Talk me through a normal weeknight, whatever happens around dinner.
D1: Honestly the hard bit is deciding. By six I just want someone to tell me what we're eating. Once I know what it is, actually cooking it is fine, that part doesn't bother me.
D1: We rotate the same five or six meals. Pasta, a stir fry, jacket potatoes, that sort of thing. I don't really plan, I just pick off the list in my head.
Interviewer: What makes a night feel like too much effort?
D1: If I'm tired and there's washing up already in the sink, that's usually when we end up getting a takeaway. It's not really about the cooking, it's walking into a messy kitchen.

sources.name: D2 — interview
paragraphs: Interviewer: When does a weeknight dinner feel easy?
D2: When I've done something at the weekend. If I batch a chilli or a curry on Sunday then Tuesday is just reheating, and I feel quite smug about it.
D2: I use a lot of shortcuts. Jarred sauce, pre-chopped stuff, the bags of frozen veg. I used to feel a bit bad about it but I've made peace with it, it still counts as cooking.
D2: My partner usually picks. I can't be bothered to have the what do you fancy conversation, so I just ask them and go with whatever they say.

sources.name: D3 — interview
paragraphs: Interviewer: What does an easy dinner look like for you?
D3: Few steps, one pan ideally, nothing where I have to keep checking a recipe. If I'm reading instructions off my phone it already feels like a lot.
D3: It depends how the day went. A bad day and the bar drops to beans on toast and I don't feel any kind of way about it. A normal day I'll actually cook something.
D3: We always eat together at the table though, even if it's something rubbish. That bit matters more to me than what it actually is.

sources.name: Photo note — D2's kitchen
sources.note: Synthetic demo data — researcher description of a participant photo.
paragraphs: D2 photographed their kitchen before starting to cook. Clear worktop, one chopping board out, a jar of sauce and a bag of frozen peas set next to the hob. The caption they added: ready to go, this is the dream.

codes.label: the deciding is the hard part
codes.memo: The effort is in choosing what to make, not in the cooking itself.

codes.label: small fixed repertoire
codes.memo: Falls back on a short rotation of known meals rather than choosing freely.

codes.label: hands the choice to someone else
codes.memo: Partner, kids or an app decides, to avoid making the call.

codes.label: tiredness sets the bar
codes.memo: How the day went decides how much effort is acceptable that night.

codes.label: batch-cooked earlier in the week
codes.memo: Work done at the weekend so a weeknight is just reheating.

codes.label: shortcut ingredients, guilt then peace
codes.memo: Jars / pre-chopped / frozen, initially felt bad about, later accepted.

codes.label: kitchen has to be clear first
codes.memo: A messy kitchen is the thing that tips a night into takeaway.

codes.label: no recipe to follow
codes.memo: Having to read instructions makes it feel like a lot.

codes.label: eating together matters
codes.memo: The shared meal is the point, more than the food.

themes.name: Easy means fewer decisions
themes.definition: When people call a dinner easy they mostly mean they didn't have to decide much. The cooking is not the burden; choosing what to cook is. They shrink the decision by leaning on a short fixed rotation of meals, or by handing the choice to someone else.
codes: the deciding is the hard part
hands the choice to someone else

themes.name: Tiredness is the real constraint
themes.definition: How much effort counts as acceptable is set by how the day went, not the clock. A bad day lowers the bar to toast with no guilt; a normal day and people cook. The main coping move is doing the work earlier — batch-cooking at the weekend.

themes.name: The kitchen has to be ready
themes.definition: A dinner feels doable or not partly before any cooking starts, based on the state of the kitchen. A sink of washing up tips a tired night into a takeaway; the photo shows the flip side, a cleared worktop with the shortcuts to hand.
codes: kitchen has to be clear first
